fork.question: How far do you want to go for your system design interviews?

cards.label: Interview core: building blocks, trade-offs, then 10+ case studies and timed mocks
stages: Foundations: how a request travels the web

cards.label: Fast track: framework, the must-know building blocks and the five classic case studies
Senior / staff depth: interview core plus consensus, distributed transactions, cloud patterns and harder case studies
stages: Foundations: how a request travels the web
Advanced case studies (payments, collaborative editing, maps, video conferencing)

outcomes.text: Estimate the capacity a stated workload needs
outcomes.observable: Given DAU, actions per user and payload sizes, produce peak QPS, storage per year and bandwidth figures within 2× of a reference answer, showing the arithmetic

outcomes.text: Turn a vague prompt into a scoped design
outcomes.observable: A written list of functional and non-functional requirements, a REST/RPC API sketch and a data model for a prompt, produced in under 10 minutes

outcomes.text: Choose and justify a data storage design
outcomes.observable: For a workload, a named store type (SQL, key-value, document, wide-column), replication mode, shard key and consistency level, each with one stated trade-off

outcomes.text: Scale the request path with standard building blocks
outcomes.observable: A high-level diagram placing load balancers, caches, CDN and queues, with a cache strategy and load-balancing choice justified against the stated reads/writes ratio

outcomes.text: Find failure modes and specify reliability mechanisms
outcomes.observable: For a given design, a list of single points of failure with a fix for each (failover, retries with backoff, circuit breaker, idempotency key) and a computed availability figure in nines

outcomes.text: Run a full system design interview under time
outcomes.observable: A complete 45-minute mock answer to a classic prompt (URL shortener, news feed, chat, ride hailing) covering requirements, estimates, API, data model, high-level design, deep dive and bottlenecks

exclusions.text: Object-oriented / low-level design (class diagrams, design patterns in code)
exclusions.why: A separate interview round with different skills; it would double the course

exclusions.text: Authentication and identity protocols in depth (OAuth 2.0 flows, OIDC, SAML, SSO)
exclusions.why: Interviews rarely go beyond 'use a token at the gateway'; covered in one security overview topic only

exclusions.text: The full cloud design patterns catalogue (valet key, strangler fig, deployment stamps, gatekeeper, etc.)
exclusions.why: Mostly migration and operations patterns that rarely come up in design interviews

exclusions.text: Storage hardware and file systems (RAID, block volumes, HDFS internals)
exclusions.why: Below the abstraction level interviewers expect; object storage is covered as a building block
Deployment tooling, not a design decision in typical interview prompts

exclusions.text: Machine-learning system design (recommendation and ranking pipelines)
exclusions.why: A specialised interview track with its own body of knowledge

exclusions.text: Vendor-specific configuration (Redis, Kafka, Nginx, AWS service settings)
exclusions.why: Interviews test the concept and trade-off, not the configuration syntax

terms.lens_reason: Every interview diagram starts with clients, an app tier and a data tier; you need the vocabulary, not the theory.
You will justify UDP for real-time media and need layer 4 vs layer 7 to discuss load balancers later.
Usually one sentence in an interview ('terminate TLS at the edge'), but you must say it correctly.
Non-functional requirements are stated as latency and throughput targets; you must not mix them up.
Quoting the right order of magnitude is how you justify a cache or a regional deployment in an interview.
Optional: mention it only when a client needs flexible data shapes; few interviews go deeper.
Useful polish that impresses interviewers, but not one of the three core capacity figures.
Interviewers expect you to tell 'slow' apart from 'does not scale' before you propose fixes.
Comes up in microservice deep dives, where a one-line mention is usually enough.
'Design a rate limiter' is a classic prompt, and rate limits appear in most API designs.
The default answer to 'which rate-limiting algorithm?', and interviewers like seeing it worked through.
Useful when the prompt is 'design a rate limiter'; elsewhere, naming one algorithm is enough.
The usual deep-dive follow-up once you put a rate limiter on a scaled-out gateway.
Named in interviews mainly as alternatives you can rule in or out
A nice-to-name option for hot read paths, rarely required
LRU is a frequent coding follow-up; policies rarely decide a design
A favourite deep-dive question once your design has a cache tier
Interviewers expect you to name the index behind each hot query in your data model and admit its write cost.
Useful vocabulary for the data-model step; interviews rarely ask for normal forms by name.
Read-heavy interview prompts almost always end with a denormalized read model; you must name its cost.
Rarely the main store in an interview; worth one sentence when a prompt is about relationships.
Comes up for multi-region prompts; most designs stay single-leader, so know when not to use it.
The usual follow-up after consistent hashing: 'how do you avoid uneven load?'
Video processing, notifications and crawlers all rely on workers pulling jobs; interviewers expect you to name them.
A strong bottleneck answer: says what happens when the queue you added can't keep up.
Interviewers often say 'Kafka' expecting you to know partitions, offsets and per-partition ordering.
A quick, credible answer to 'what if a message keeps failing?' in reliability deep dives.
Lets you justify the push mechanism instead of reflexively saying WebSockets.
A senior-sounding fix for keeping caches and search indexes consistent with the database.
Comes up as a named pattern in senior interviews; enough to recognise it and know when not to use it.
Precise vocabulary helps you state non-functional requirements crisply.
A good extra to name after a circuit breaker; rarely asked about on its own.
Interviewers often ask whether to split services; you need the trade-off in one breath.
Comes up when a design spans two databases; know why you usually avoid it.
The expected answer for cross-service payments and bookings in interviews.
Asked when a design has one writer or one scheduler; split brain is the key word.
Name-level knowledge is enough for most interviews; senior rounds may probe it.
Turns vague 'highly available' requirements into numbers interviewers respect.
A short monitoring mention closes a design answer well; depth is rarely probed.
Worth naming when microservices appear in your design.
Interviewers expect one crisp sentence on where authentication and authorization happen; protocol flows are excluded.
Region-loss questions come up in senior rounds; RPO/RTO is the expected vocabulary.
Interviewers often bring it up in crawler, dedup and storage deep dives. It is a cheap way to show depth.
A frequent standalone prompt, and a common deep dive inside other designs.
Common at mid and senior levels. It checks replication, quorum and hashing together.
A classic prompt that tests queues, deduplication and politeness. It comes up less often than feed or chat.
A popular prompt. It rewards knowing the trie plus offline aggregation pattern.
A common prompt that reuses feed design and shows a clean media upload path.
A frequent prompt. Most of the marks come from the CDN and transcoding pipeline.
Often mentioned as the alternative to geohash. Knowing the trade-off is usually enough.
A common mid-level prompt that tests queues, retries and deduplication.
Increasingly common, and it is the best prompt for showing correctness under failure. Enrichment: idempotency and retries themselves are taught in earlier stages.
Booking prompts (Ticketmaster, Airbnb, flights) are popular, and contention is the deep dive interviewers expect.
